name: Digital Credit Assessment
description: Digital credit assessment uses recorded financial information to support judgments about repayment risk. Iran has documented experience with electronic credit-information sharing, although historical evidence does not establish the coverage, accuracy, or fairness of systems operating today.

seo.title: Digital Credit Assessment in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s credit-information infrastructure, the distinction between reports and lending decisions, and the evidence still needed to assess performance.

content.heading: A documented foundation for digital assessment
content.content:
Iran’s digital credit-assessment infrastructure predates many contemporary lending applications. The World Bank’s Doing Business 2020 economy profile recorded online access to borrowers’ credit information for banks and financial institutions. It also recorded credit scores as a service offered by the credit bureau. These findings establish a historical foundation for electronically supported assessment; they do not describe every lender or certify present-day service quality. [s1]

The profile distinguished a credit bureau from a credit registry rather than treating them as a single database. Its questionnaire recorded the distribution of information about both firms and individuals, and both positive and negative credit information. This distinction matters: a record of successful repayment conveys something different from a record limited to arrears. The report also identified differences between bureau and registry practices, so their functions should not be assumed to be interchangeable. [s1]

content.heading: Information supports a decision
content.content:
Iran Credit Scoring describes its role as aggregating credit-related information supplied by participating members and providing a more complete risk profile of prospective or existing customers. Its institutional account presents credit reporting as a way to help providers make lending decisions more quickly and objectively. This is the company’s description of its purpose, rather than independent evidence that those outcomes have been achieved. [s2]

The relationship is important for understanding the technology. Members contribute information; the bureau assembles a report or risk profile; the credit provider uses that information in its own assessment. A report is therefore an input to lending, rather than evidence that a particular applicant will receive credit. The company’s description also encompasses individuals and corporate entities, reminding readers that credit-information services extend beyond consumer borrowing. [s2]

content.heading: What the available evidence does not establish
content.content:
The inspected World Bank profile is a historical account of information infrastructure. It does not establish how accurately a current model predicts repayment, whether different groups experience different error rates, or whether electronically assessed applications lead to more affordable borrowing. Likewise, the provider’s institutional description explains its intended function without supplying an independently evaluated account of those outcomes. [s1][s2]

A fuller assessment of Iran’s digital-credit sector requires current documentation of data coverage, model validation, correction procedures, and lending outcomes. Until that evidence is inspected, claims that digital scoring has eliminated collateral requirements, expanded credit nationwide, or made decisions unbiased would exceed the sources reviewed here.

Current model inputs, predictive performance, validation methods, and demographic fairness.

name: Crowdfunding
description: Crowdfunding brings contributions from multiple participants together through a platform to finance a project or purpose. In Iran’s business-finance sector, industry research describes platforms connecting investors with enterprises seeking capital, while emphasizing repayment risk and limited liquidity.

seo.title: Crowdfunding in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iranian business crowdfunding, its different models, platform relationships, and the distinction between projected returns and investment outcomes.

content.heading: One term, different financial relationships
content.content:
Crowdfunding is an umbrella term. TechRasa Insight’s Iranian industry report distinguishes donation, reward, debt, equity, and litigation-finance models. These involve different relationships: a donation does not promise repayment, a reward may involve a product or service, and equity involves ownership. The report identifies Iranian business-platform examples within its debt-oriented category, where capital is supplied against an expectation of repayment and projected profit. This is an industry classification, not a substitute for examining a project’s legal contract. [s1]

The report links the development of Iranian platforms to enterprises’ working-capital needs and investors’ search for alternatives during inflation and currency depreciation. These are the report’s explanations of demand rather than independently demonstrated causal effects. Its account places business crowdfunding within the wider financing system, rather than treating every online fundraising campaign as the same financial product. [s1]

content.heading: The platform and the financed business
content.content:
A platform’s identity and a project’s obligations answer different questions. Dongi’s public website describes the service as operating under the supervision of Tose'e Firouzeh Portfolio Management and cites a Farabourse authorization. Farabourse is Iran’s over-the-counter securities exchange. This establishes what the operator publicly claims about its institutional relationship; an independently inspected regulator register is still needed to verify authorization at a particular date. [s2]

A September 2026 industry directory similarly presents platforms alongside associated financial institutions. It cautions that a platform authorization does not guarantee the principal or profit of every project. Its discussion also distinguishes projected returns, payment schedules, project duration, and the form of security. Those distinctions make the individual financing arrangement central to understanding what a participant is being offered. [s3]

content.heading: Projected profit is not a completed outcome
content.content:
TechRasa’s report identifies limited liquidity and default risk as constraints on the sector. In plain English, liquidity concerns whether participation can be converted back into cash when needed; default concerns a financed enterprise failing to meet its payment obligations. The report discusses stronger guarantees and possible secondary-market development, but these should not be read as proof that every investment is immediately transferable or protected against loss. [s1]

The September 2026 directory emphasizes that quoted returns belong to particular projects, rather than representing a permanent rate for an entire platform. It also notes that payment timing varies. A short project’s stated return, an annualized equivalent, and a realized payment are therefore different descriptions and cannot be compared without their original terms. [s3]

The available evidence supports describing crowdfunding as a route connecting enterprises and investors through digital platforms. It does not yet support a verified account here of market-wide realized returns, recovery rates, or current authorization conditions. Those gaps matter more than a promotional ranking of platforms.

name: Digital Investment
description: Digital investment encompasses online interfaces through which people access investment products and monitor holdings. Iranian examples include applications offering investment funds, while industry research distinguishes these distribution services from portfolio management and the creation of financial products.

seo.title: Digital Investment in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Discover how Iranian investment platforms present funds and other products, and why app access, investment management, and asset risk are separate questions.

content.heading: An interface to investment products
content.content:
An investment application is a way of accessing products, rather than an asset class in itself. TechRasa Insight places online asset platforms within wealth technology: digital services concerned with investment access, asset management, advice, and financial planning. Its Iranian market classification separates product creation, transaction intermediation, and personalized portfolio management. This is a useful distinction because a convenient interface does not by itself establish who manages the underlying money. [s1]

The report also distinguishes platforms associated with financial groups from aggregators. Its broader landscape includes investment funds, precious metals, cryptocurrency, and other offerings, but this does not mean every application supplies every category or operates under the same institutional arrangements. The classification describes a varied market rather than a single interchangeable investment service. [s1]

content.heading: A documented Iranian example
content.content:
Kian Digital’s website presents an investment application and lists fund categories that include fixed income, gold, and equities. Its own company profile describes an integrated mobile application offering banking and investment-management services. These materials establish the provider’s advertised service scope; they are not independent verification of investment performance, customer satisfaction, or the suitability of a particular fund. [s2][s3]

The website discusses investment as a response to inflation and presents options intended for relatively small amounts of money. It also acknowledges that different investment choices have different risks and returns. The relevant editorial point is that a shared interface can present products with substantially different financial characteristics. An app’s branding cannot replace the underlying product description. [s2]

An earlier company post describes remote registration and identity verification for activating investment funds, undertaken with an external technology partner. It is evidence of a company-announced onboarding capability, rather than an independent test of identity controls or a guarantee that every user can complete the process remotely. [s4]

content.heading: Separating available services from future possibilities
content.content:
TechRasa’s report discusses personalization, artificial intelligence, tokenization, and closer connections between investment products and banking services as prospective developments. These scenarios should retain their forward-looking character. They do not establish that automated personalized advice, tokenized ownership, or a particular banking integration was already available across Iran’s investment market. [s1]

For the same reason, descriptions such as digital, intelligent, or integrated should be interpreted alongside a specific service claim. Kian’s materials document an application, product listings, and announced onboarding functions; they do not provide enough evidence here to establish independently how investments are selected for each customer or whether an automated recommendation improves outcomes. [s2][s3][s4]

A fuller account needs product-level documentation and verified institutional responsibilities. The evidence inspected supports an explanation of digital distribution and advertised capabilities, while leaving market-wide adoption, investment results, and current legal arrangements for further research.
